issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence in this profile. It is much more characteristic of sexual trauma or interpersonal violation with a strong disgust/shame component, and here there are no supporting memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items that would make this appraisal clinically coherent. The remaining items describe intrusive, alien, uncontrolled traumatic memory and general danger/body-reactivity beliefs, which fit severe PTSD, but the contamination item stands out as a trauma-incongruent appraisal.

vignette: Three years ago, during a domestic call in a quiet subdivision, Clara’s patrol partner, a man she had trusted with her life for four years, drew his service weapon and fired twice into an unarmed suspect who was simply backing away with his hands raised. The crack of the gun, the wet thud against the pavement, and the sudden, heavy silence that followed are the anchors of her current reality. She had arrived expecting a routine welfare check, but the scene fractured into something unrecognizable. The department’s quick pivot to a justified report didn’t just erase the incident; it severed her faith in the badge and the man standing beside her. Since that night, Clara’s days have become a series of careful negotiations with her own mind. She tries to maintain her patrol routes, but the precinct has become a landscape of hidden triggers. The rhythmic clatter of the dispatch radio in her cruiser still makes her grip the steering wheel until her knuckles bleach white. When a call comes in for a possible assault, her breath catches before the vehicle even moves. She has come to believe her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe, a traitorous instrument that floods with adrenaline the moment she hears a similar siren, making her hands tremble as if she were the one in combat. What frightens her most is the certainty that the world is a dangerous place, a environment where any routine can instantly curdle into violence. She is certain that if she lets her guard down, even for a second, she will be caught off guard again. A fleeting tightness in her jaw when she passes the local armory is something she notes but rarely addresses, a minor physical echo she leaves behind. This constant state of perceived threat does not stay contained. Every time she tells herself she must stay alert, the mental walls erode. Her conviction that the world is a dangerous place and her belief that her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe act as direct invitations to the past. The moment she feels that familiar spike of fear, the memory forces its way into her mind when she does not want it to. She is no longer in the patrol car; she is back on that cracked driveway, the memory feeling completely real across all her senses at once. She smells the copper tang of blood, hears the suspect’s muffled pleas, and sees the partner’s steady breathing, the recollection unfolding with such immediacy that she drops her coffee cup without realizing she has let go. When those intrusions take hold, they do not simply pass. The uncontrolled access of the event strips away any distance between past and present, cementing her worst fears. Each time the memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to her, it deepens her conviction that the world is a dangerous place. She is certain that her own physiology is a liability, that the rapid pulse and shallow breathing are proof she cannot rely on herself to stay protected. The betrayal by someone she trusted becomes vivid again, and she retreats from her boyfriend at home, sleeping on the couch because the sudden closeness feels like a threat rather than comfort. Over the past eighteen months, these habits have carved a deep groove. She requests desk duty, but even the quiet of the records room offers no relief. She has stopped attending the weekly union meetings where they still talk about the partner who fired those shots, and her partner has stopped asking why she checks the locks three times before bed. She came to the clinic hoping to find a way to quiet the noise in her head, to separate herself from a past that feels like it is constantly bleeding into her present, terrified that without intervention, the loop of fear and flashback will continue to steal her life and her career.
